claim: Pulmonary fibrosis is a fatal lung disease characterized by fibrotic foci and inflammatory infiltrates.
source: Pulmonary fibrosis is a fatal lung disease characterized by fibrotic foci and inflammatory infiltrates.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about pulmonary fibrosis presented in the abstract, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Short telomeres can impair tissue regeneration.
source: Short telomeres can impair tissue regeneration and are found both in hereditary and sporadic cases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Short telomeres are found both in hereditary and sporadic cases of pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Short telomeres can impair tissue regeneration and are found both in hereditary and sporadic cases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alder et al., 2008 and Armanios et al., 2007 in the manuscript.

claim: Telomerase expression using AAV9 vectors shows therapeutic effects in a mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis owing to a low-dose bleomycin insult and short telomeres.
source: We show here that telomerase expression using AAV9 vectors shows therapeutic effects in a mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis owing to a low-dose bleomycin insult and short telomeres.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: AAV9 preferentially targets regenerative alveolar type II cells (ATII).
source: AAV9 preferentially targets regenerative alveolar type II cells (ATII).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that more than 80% of all GFP-positive lung cells were ATII cells (Figure 1A).

claim: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show improved lung function at 1–3 weeks after viral treatment.
source: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show improved lung function and lower inflammation and fibrosis at 1–3 weeks after viral treatment, and improvement or disappearance of the fibrosis at 8 weeks after treatment.
evidence: This is supported by spirometry data showing improved LR/Cdyn ratios (Figure 1E).

claim: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show lower inflammation and fibrosis at 1–3 weeks after viral treatment.
source: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show improved lung function and lower inflammation and fibrosis at 1–3 weeks after viral treatment, and improvement or disappearance of the fibrosis at 8 weeks after treatment.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurements (Figure 2J,K) and histological analysis (Figure 2A,B).

claim: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show improvement or disappearance of the fibrosis at 8 weeks after treatment.
source: AAV9-Tert-treated mice show improved lung function and lower inflammation and fibrosis at 1–3 weeks after viral treatment, and improvement or disappearance of the fibrosis at 8 weeks after treatment.
evidence: This is supported by histopathological analysis showing 50% of Tert-treated mice were completely free of fibrotic lesions at 8 weeks (Figure 1G,H).

claim: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres in ATII cells.
source: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres and increased proliferation of ATII cells, as well as lower DNA damage, apoptosis, and senescence.
evidence: This is supported by Immuno-FISH data showing ATII cells from AAV9-Tert treated mice had the same telomere length as non-ATII cells (Figure 3E-G).

claim: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to increased proliferation of ATII cells.
source: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres and increased proliferation of ATII cells, as well as lower DNA damage, apoptosis, and senescence.
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining showing 2.5-fold increase in Ki67 positive ATII cells (Figure 3H-K).

claim: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to lower DNA damage in ATII cells.
source: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres and increased proliferation of ATII cells, as well as lower DNA damage, apoptosis, and senescence.
evidence: This is supported by γH2AX staining showing reduced DNA damage (Figure 3A,B,C,D).

claim: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to lower apoptosis in lung cells.
source: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres and increased proliferation of ATII cells, as well as lower DNA damage, apoptosis, and senescence.
evidence: This is supported by caspase 3 staining showing decreased apoptosis (Figure 3A,B).

claim: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to lower senescence in lung cells.
source: AAV9-Tert treatment leads to longer telomeres and increased proliferation of ATII cells, as well as lower DNA damage, apoptosis, and senescence.
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-galactosidase staining showing senescent cells were undetectable in AAV9-Tert treated lungs (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Transcriptome analysis of ATII cells confirms downregulation of fibrosis and inflammation pathways after AAV9-Tert treatment.
source: Transcriptome analysis of ATII cells confirms downregulation of fibrosis and inflammation pathways.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis showing downregulation of TGF-β, NF-KappaB, IL2 and TNF signaling pathways (Figure 5H-K).

claim: Mammalian telomeres are protective structures at ends of chromosomes that consist of TTAGGG repeats bound by a six-protein complex known as shelterin.
source: Mammalian telomeres are protective structures at ends of chromosomes that consist of TTAGGG repeats bound by a six-protein complex known as shelterin (Blackburn, 2001; de Lange, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blackburn, 2001 and de Lange, 2005.

claim: A minimum length of telomeric repeats is necessary for shelterin binding and telomere protection.
source: A minimum length of telomeric repeats is necessary for shelterin binding and telomere protection (Blackburn, 2001; de Lange, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blackburn, 2001 and de Lange, 2005.

claim: Telomerase is an enzyme composed of two subunits, the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the RNA component (Terc).
source: Telomerase is an enzyme composed of two subunits, the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the RNA component (Terc), which is used as template for the de novo addition of telomeric repeats to chromosome ends (Greider and Blackburn, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greider and Blackburn, 1985.

claim: Telomerase RNA component (Terc) is used as template for the de novo addition of telomeric repeats to chromosome ends.
source: Telomerase is an enzyme composed of two subunits, the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the RNA component (Terc), which is used as template for the de novo addition of telomeric repeats to chromosome ends (Greider and Blackburn, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Greider and Blackburn, 1985.

claim: Adult tissues, including the stem cell compartments, do not have sufficient telomerase activity to compensate for the progressive telomere shortening associated with cell division throughout lifespan.
source: Adult tissues, including the stem cell compartments, do not have sufficient telomerase activity to compensate for the progressive telomere shortening associated with cell division throughout lifespan (Canela et al., 2007; Flores et al., 2008; Harley et al., 1990; Vera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canela et al., 2007; Flores et al., 2008; Harley et al., 1990; Vera et al., 2012.

claim: When telomeres reach a critically short length, this triggers activation of a persistent DNA damage response at telomeres and the subsequent induction of cellular senescence or apoptosis.
source: When telomeres reach a critically short length, this triggers activation of a persistent DNA damage response at telomeres and the subsequent induction of cellular senescence or apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: Progressive shortening of telomeres with increasing age is considered one of the hallmarks of aging both in mice and humans.
source: Indeed, this progressive shortening of telomeres with increasing age is considered one of the hallmarks of aging both in mice and humans (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Critical telomere shortening at the stem cell compartments results in the loss of the regenerative capacity of these compartments eventually compromising tissue renewal and homeostasis.
source: In particular, critical telomere shortening at the stem cell compartments results in the loss of the regenerative capacity of these compartments eventually compromising tissue renewal and homeostasis (Blasco, 2007; Flores et al., 2005; Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blasco, 2007; Flores et al., 2005; Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: The rate of telomere shortening throughout lifespan has been shown to be influenced both by genetic factors and environmental factors.
source: Interestingly, the rate of telomere shortening throughout lifespan has been shown to be influenced both by genetic factors (ie., mutations in genes necessary for telomere maintenance) and environmental factors (ie., cigarette smoke has a negative effect) (Armanios, 2013; King et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Armanios, 2013 and King et al., 2011.

claim: Cigarette smoke has a negative effect on telomere shortening.
source: Interestingly, the rate of telomere shortening throughout lifespan has been shown to be influenced both by genetic factors (ie., mutations in genes necessary for telomere maintenance) and environmental factors (ie., cigarette smoke has a negative effect) (Armanios, 2013; King et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Armanios, 2013 and King et al., 2011.

claim: Increased TERT expression in the context of cancer resistant transgenic mice was sufficient to delay aging and extend mouse longevity by 40%.
source: In support of critical telomere shortening being a determinant of aging and longevity, increased TERT expression in the context of cancer resistant transgenic mice was sufficient to delay aging and extend mouse longevity by 40% (Tomás-Loba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tomás-Loba et al., 2008.

claim: Treatment with Tert gene therapy using non-integrative AAV9 vectors of adult mice was able to delay aging and increase longevity by decreasing age-related pathologies.
source: In particular, treatment with Tert gene therapy using non-integrative AAV9 vectors of adult mice was able to delay aging and increase longevity by decreasing age-related pathologies such as osteoporosis, glucose intolerance, as well as neuromuscular and cognitive decline.
evidence: This is supported by the context referring to Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012.

claim: The onset of cancer was delayed in Tert treated mice.
source: Furthermore, the onset of cancer was also delayed in the Tert treated mice (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012.

claim: AAV9-Tert delivery specifically to the heart was sufficient to significantly increase mouse survival and heart function upon myocardial infarction.
source: More recently, AAV9-Tert delivery specifically to the heart was sufficient to significantly increase mouse survival and heart function upon myocardial infarction, which was concomitant with decreased fibrosis and increased cardiac myocyte proliferation (Bär et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bär et al., 2014.

claim: AAV9-Tert delivery to the heart was concomitant with decreased fibrosis and increased cardiac myocyte proliferation.
source: More recently, AAV9-Tert delivery specifically to the heart was sufficient to significantly increase mouse survival and heart function upon myocardial infarction, which was concomitant with decreased fibrosis and increased cardiac myocyte proliferation (Bär et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bär et al., 2014.

claim: Extreme telomere shortening can occur prematurely in individuals with mutations in telomerase and other telomere maintenance genes causing the so-called telomere syndromes.
source: Extreme telomere shortening can occur prematurely in individuals with mutations in telomerase and other telomere maintenance genes causing the so-called telomere syndromes, which include dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia and pulmonary fibrosis, among others (for a review see [Armanios and Blackburn, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armanios and Blackburn, 2012.

claim: Telomere syndromes include dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia and pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Extreme telomere shortening can occur prematurely in individuals with mutations in telomerase and other telomere maintenance genes causing the so-called telomere syndromes, which include dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia and pulmonary fibrosis, among others (for a review see [Armanios and Blackburn, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armanios and Blackburn, 2012.

claim: Telomere syndromes are characterized by premature loss of the regenerative capacity of tissues, affecting both high and low proliferation tissues.
source: These syndromes are characterized by premature loss of the regenerative capacity of tissues, affecting both high and low proliferation tissues (Armanios and Blackburn, 2012; Holohan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Armanios and Blackburn, 2012 and Holohan et al., 2014.

claim: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is the most common condition associated with telomere dysfunction in humans.
source: Among the telomere syndromes, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is the most common condition associated with telomere dysfunction in humans (Armanios, 2013; Armanios and Blackburn, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Armanios, 2013 and Armanios and Blackburn, 2012.

claim: Both familial and sporadic cases of IPF have been linked to telomerase mutations, either in TERT or TERC.
source: Both familial and sporadic cases have been linked to telomerase mutations, either in TERT or TERC (Alder et al., 2008; Armanios et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alder et al., 2008 and Armanios et al., 2007.

claim: Mutations in TERT and TERC account for 8–15% of familial IPF cases.
source: In particular, mutations in TERT and TERC account for 8–15% of familial and 1–3% of sporadic cases (Alder et al., 2008; Armanios, 2013; Armanios et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alder et al., 2008; Armanios, 2013; and Armanios et al., 2007.

claim: Mutations in TERT and TERC account for 1–3% of sporadic IPF cases.
source: In particular, mutations in TERT and TERC account for 8–15% of familial and 1–3% of sporadic cases (Alder et al., 2008; Armanios, 2013; Armanios et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alder et al., 2008; Armanios, 2013; and Armanios et al., 2007.

claim: Sporadic cases of IPF, not associated with telomerase mutations, also show shorter telomeres compared to age-matched controls.
source: Interestingly, sporadic cases of IPF, not associated with telomerase mutations, also show shorter telomeres compared to age-matched controls, with 10% of the patients showing telomeres as short as the telomerase mutation carriers (Alder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alder et al., 2008.

claim: 10% of sporadic IPF patients show telomeres as short as the telomerase mutation carriers.
source: Interestingly, sporadic cases of IPF, not associated with telomerase mutations, also show shorter telomeres compared to age-matched controls, with 10% of the patients showing telomeres as short as the telomerase mutation carriers (Alder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alder et al., 2008.

claim: Telomerase mutations have been found in up to 1% of smokers showing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
source: Telomerase mutations have also been found in up to 1% of smokers showing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), also leading to abnormally short telomeres (Stanley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stanley et al., 2015.

claim: Telomerase mutations in COPD patients lead to abnormally short telomeres.
source: Telomerase mutations have also been found in up to 1% of smokers showing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), also leading to abnormally short telomeres (Stanley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stanley et al., 2015.

claim: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is still a life-threatening lung degenerative disease, with few available therapeutic options.
source: Unfortunately, in spite of its prevalence, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is still a life-threatening lung degenerative disease, with few available therapeutic options (King et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King et al., 2011.

claim: Nintedanib and pirfenidone show anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic activity.
source: As an example, the recently FDA-approved drugs, nintedanib and pirfenidone, show anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic activity (Ahluwalia et al., 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; King et al., 2014), and slow IPF progression but are not curative (Hunninghake, 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; King et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahluwalia et al., 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; and King et al., 2014.

claim: Nintedanib and pirfenidone slow IPF progression but are not curative.
source: As an example, the recently FDA-approved drugs, nintedanib and pirfenidone, show anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic activity (Ahluwalia et al., 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; King et al., 2014), and slow IPF progression but are not curative (Hunninghake, 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; King et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hunninghake, 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; and King et al., 2014.

claim: Lung transplantation is the only curative therapeutic option in less than 5% of IPF patients with severe disease.
source: Indeed, to date, lung transplantation is the only curative therapeutic option in less than 5% of IPF patients with severe disease (Lama, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lama, 2009.

claim: Induction of acute pulmonary fibrosis with high doses of bleomycin in mice has been the most widely used preclinical model.
source: Induction of acute pulmonary fibrosis with high doses of bleomycin in mice has been the most widely used preclinical model, although the disease spontaneously reverses in this model after 2–3 weeks (Mouratis and Aidinis, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mouratis and Aidinis, 2011.

claim: The disease spontaneously reverses in the high-dose bleomycin mouse model after 2–3 weeks.
source: Induction of acute pulmonary fibrosis with high doses of bleomycin in mice has been the most widely used preclinical model, although the disease spontaneously reverses in this model after 2–3 weeks (Mouratis and Aidinis, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mouratis and Aidinis, 2011.

claim: Telomerase-deficient mice with short telomeres do not spontaneously develop pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Furthermore, telomerase-deficient mice with short telomeres do not spontaneously develop pulmonary fibrosis (Alder et al., 2011), suggesting that additional insults contribute to the disease in addition to the genetic defects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alder et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment with low doses of bleomycin (0.5 mg/kg BW), which normally do not lead to pulmonary fibrosis in wild-type mice, results in full-blown progressive pulmonary fibrosis in telomerase deficient mice.
source: In support of this notion, we recently demonstrated that treatment with low doses of bleomycin (0.5 mg/kg BW), which normally do not lead to pulmonary fibrosis in wild-type mice, however, results in full-blown progressive pulmonary fibrosis in telomerase deficient mice (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: 3% of total lung cells are transduced by AAV9-eGFP.
source: We found transduction of 3% (GFP positive cells) of total lung cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 13.4% of total lung cells are ATII cells (Sftpc-positive cells).
source: We first observed that 13.4% of total lung cells were ATII cells (Sftpc-positive cells) (Figure 1A), which is in line with the 12–15% reported abundance of ATII cells in whole lung cell population (Dobbs, 1990; Van der Velden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1A, and is consistent with literature values.

claim: 17% of total ATII cells are transduced by AAV9-eGFP.
source: Importantly, we observed that 17% of total ATII cells were transduced by AAV9-eGFP (GFP-positive) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: More than 80% of all the GFP-positive lung cells are ATII cells.
source: Indeed, more than 80% of all the GFP-positive lung cells were ATII cells (Figure 1A), indicating that AAV9 has a specific tropism for these cells.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AAV9 has a specific tropism for ATII cells.
source: Indeed, more than 80% of all the GFP-positive lung cells were ATII cells (Figure 1A), indicating that AAV9 has a specific tropism for these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that 80% of GFP-positive cells are ATII cells.

claim: Approximately 50% of G2 Tert-/- mice treated with low bleomycin dose showed an abnormal radiographic pattern presenting reticular opacities suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Approximately 50% of the mice showed an abnormal radiographic pattern presenting reticular opacities suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is experimental data from the current study, also referenced to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: One week after AAV9-Tert viral treatment, all abnormal radiological images in AAV9-Tert treated mice regressed in size.
source: Interestingly, only one week after viral treatment, CT imaging showed that all abnormal radiological images in AAV9-Tert treated mice regressed in size, while they further increased in size in mice treated with the empty vector (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: One week after viral treatment, abnormal radiological images in mice treated with the empty vector further increased in size.
source: Interestingly, only one week after viral treatment, CT imaging showed that all abnormal radiological images in AAV9-Tert treated mice regressed in size, while they further increased in size in mice treated with the empty vector (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: At week seven after treatment with the viral vectors, the affected CT lung volume in the AAV9-Tert treated mice corresponds to only 5% of total lung volume.
source: Importantly, at week seven after treatment with the viral vectors (week nine after the induction of fibrosis with bleomycin), the affected CT lung volume in the AAV9-Tert treated mice corresponds to only 5% of total lung volume, while at this point mice treated with the empty vector still exhibited 40% of total lung volume affected as indicated by CT (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: At week seven after treatment with the viral vectors, mice treated with the empty vector still exhibited 40% of total lung volume affected as indicated by CT.
source: Importantly, at week seven after treatment with the viral vectors (week nine after the induction of fibrosis with bleomycin), the affected CT lung volume in the AAV9-Tert treated mice corresponds to only 5% of total lung volume, while at this point mice treated with the empty vector still exhibited 40% of total lung volume affected as indicated by CT (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Lung function in AAV9-Tert treated mice became similar to that of healthy mice non-treated with bleomycin at two weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Importantly, pulmonary function in AAV9-Tert treated mice became similar to that of healthy mice non-treated with bleomycin at two weeks post-viral treatment and was maintained thereafter, illustrating the efficacy of the treatment at restoring lung health.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from spirometry measurements.

claim: Mice treated with AAV9-Empty show significant higher LR/Cdyn values as compared to healthy and to AAV9-Tert, indicating a worsened pulmonary function.
source: In contrast, mice treated with AAV9-Empty show significant higher LR/Cdyn values as compared to healthy and to AAV9-Tert, indicating a worsened pulmonary function (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At week 8 after treatment with the viral vectors, all mice treated with the empty vector showed severe fibrosis as indicated by more than 30% of the lung parenchyma affected by fibrosis.
source: We found that at week 8 after treatment with the viral vectors (week 10 after the induction of fibrosis), all mice treated with the empty vector showed severe fibrosis as indicated by more than 30% of the lung parenchyma affected by fibrosis (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: None of the AAV9-Tert treated mice showed severe fibrosis at week 8 after viral treatment.
source: In contrast, none of the AAV9-Tert treated mice showed severe fibrosis at this point.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from histopathological analysis.

claim: 50% of AAV9-Tert treated mice presented mild fibrosis at week 8 after viral treatment.
source: Instead, 50% of Tert-treated mice presented mild fibrosis lesions and 50% were completely free of fibrotic lesions (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: 50% of AAV9-Tert treated mice were completely free of fibrotic lesions at week 8 after viral treatment.
source: Instead, 50% of Tert-treated mice presented mild fibrosis lesions and 50% were completely free of fibrotic lesions (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice presented one-third less collagen deposition compared to mice treated with the empty vector.
source: Picrosirius red staining of lungs to determine collagen deposition, confirmed that AAV9-Tert treated mice presented one-third less collagen deposition compared to mice treated with the empty vector (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Bleomycin treated lungs present a 2-fold increase in the amount of collagen peptides containing hydroxyproline compared to control lungs not treated with bleomycin.
source: The results show that bleomycin treated lungs present a 2-fold increase in the amount of collagen peptides containing hydroxyproline compared to control lungs not treated with bleomycin (w/o bleomycin) in agreement with induction of fibrosis by bleomycin in Tert-deficient mice (Figure 2C, left panel), thus validating this method for quantification of fibrosis.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2C, left panel.

claim: At 8 weeks after viral treatment, AAV9-Tert treated lungs showed 2-fold lower content in collagen peptides containing hydroxyproline compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs.
source: At 8 weeks after viral treatment (10 weeks post bleomycin treatment), AAV9-Tert treated lungs showed 2-fold lower content in collagen peptides containing hydroxyproline compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs, indicating that telomerase treatment improves collagen removal (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2C, right panel.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed approximately 50% lower levels of procollagen compared to the controls at 3 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Analysis of total procollagen levels in the lung using western blot analysis also showed approximately 50% and 30% lower levels of procollagen in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to the controls at 3 and 8 weeks post-viral treatment, respectively, suggesting that Tert gene therapy leads to a more rapid removal of fiber deposition (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed approximately 30% lower levels of procollagen compared to the controls at 8 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Analysis of total procollagen levels in the lung using western blot analysis also showed approximately 50% and 30% lower levels of procollagen in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to the controls at 3 and 8 weeks post-viral treatment, respectively, suggesting that Tert gene therapy leads to a more rapid removal of fiber deposition (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated lungs showed significantly less αSMA-positive myofibroblasts compared to empty vector-treated mice.
source: In line with lower collagen, AAV9-Tert treated lungs also showed significantly less αSMA-positive myofibroblasts compared to empty vector-treated mice, in agreement with the fact that these cells are associated with collagen deposition in human IPF patients (Figure 2F,G), thus suggesting an inactivation of fibrotic foci upon Tert treatment.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: αSMA-positive myofibroblasts are associated with collagen deposition in human IPF patients.
source: In line with lower collagen, AAV9-Tert treated lungs also showed significantly less αSMA-positive myofibroblasts compared to empty vector-treated mice, in agreement with the fact that these cells are associated with collagen deposition in human IPF patients (Figure 2F,G), thus suggesting an inactivation of fibrotic foci upon Tert treatment.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed significantly less macrophage infiltrates in their remaining fibrotic areas compared with AAV9-Empty treated mice.
source: Finally, also in agreement with fibrosis regression and tissue healing in mice treated with telomerase, AAV9-Tert treated mice showed significantly less macrophage infiltrates as detected by F4/80 staining in their remaining fibrotic areas compared with AAV9-Empty treated mice (Figure 2H,I), suggestive of decreased inflammation.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2H,I.

claim: At 3 weeks after viral treatment, AAV9-Tert treated mice showed significantly lower levels of cytokines compared to the cohort treated with the empty vector.
source: In particular, already at 3 weeks after viral treatment, AAV9-Tert treated mice showed significantly lower levels of these cytokines compared to the cohort treated with the empty vector and this was maintained at 8 weeks after viral treatment, indicating the efficacy of the therapy in dampening the inflammatory response (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Lower cytokine levels in AAV9-Tert treated mice were maintained at 8 weeks after viral treatment.
source: In particular, already at 3 weeks after viral treatment, AAV9-Tert treated mice showed significantly lower levels of these cytokines compared to the cohort treated with the empty vector and this was maintained at 8 weeks after viral treatment, indicating the efficacy of the therapy in dampening the inflammatory response (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Short dysfunctional telomeres trigger a persistent DNA damage response (DDR) characterized by increased γH2AX foci.
source: Short dysfunctional telomeres have been previously shown to trigger a persistent DNA damage response (DDR) characterized by increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 cell arrest and senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis (Hemann et al., 2000; Meier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hemann et al., 2000 and Meier et al., 2007.

claim: Short dysfunctional telomeres trigger increased expression of p21 and p53 cell arrest and senescence markers.
source: Short dysfunctional telomeres have been previously shown to trigger a persistent DNA damage response (DDR) characterized by increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 cell arrest and senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis (Hemann et al., 2000; Meier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hemann et al., 2000 and Meier et al., 2007.

claim: Short dysfunctional telomeres trigger induction of apoptosis.
source: Short dysfunctional telomeres have been previously shown to trigger a persistent DNA damage response (DDR) characterized by increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 cell arrest and senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis (Hemann et al., 2000; Meier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hemann et al., 2000 and Meier et al., 2007.

claim: Mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres show increased γH2AX foci in the lungs.
source: Indeed, we previously described that mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres also show increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis in the lungs (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: Mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres show increased expression of p21 and p53 senescence markers in the lungs.
source: Indeed, we previously described that mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres also show increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis in the lungs (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: Mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres show induction of apoptosis in the lungs.
source: Indeed, we previously described that mice with pulmonary fibrosis owing to short telomeres also show increased γH2AX foci, increased expression of p21 and p53 senescence markers, as well as induction of apoptosis in the lungs (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: The lungs of AAV9-Tert treated mice have a significant reduction of DNA damage at 3 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Interestingly, analysis of these molecular markers in the lungs of treated mice at two time points after viral treatment shows that the lungs of AAV9-Tert treated mice have a significant reduction of DNA damage already at 3 weeks post-viral treatment which is also maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment (endpoint of the experiment), as indicated by lower percentage of cells positive for γH2AX compared to mice treated with empty vector (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The reduction of DNA damage in AAV9-Tert treated mice is maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Interestingly, analysis of these molecular markers in the lungs of treated mice at two time points after viral treatment shows that the lungs of AAV9-Tert treated mice have a significant reduction of DNA damage already at 3 weeks post-viral treatment which is also maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment (endpoint of the experiment), as indicated by lower percentage of cells positive for γH2AX compared to mice treated with empty vector (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed a significant reduction in the abundance of p21 and p53-positive cells at 3 weeks after viral treatment.
source: Consistently, we also found a significant reduction in the abundance of p21 and p53-positive cells in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to those treated with the empty vector as early as 3 weeks after viral treatment and again these lower levels were maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Lower levels of p21 and p53-positive cells in AAV9-Tert treated mice were maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Consistently, we also found a significant reduction in the abundance of p21 and p53-positive cells in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to those treated with the empty vector as early as 3 weeks after viral treatment and again these lower levels were maintained at 8 weeks post-viral treatment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed a significant decrease in caspase 3-positive cells at 3 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Moreover, we also observed a significant decrease in caspase 3-positive cells at both time points (3 and 8 weeks post-viral treatment) in the lungs of Tert-treated mice compared to the empty-treated cohort (Figure 3A,B), indicative of decreased apoptosis.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated mice showed a significant decrease in caspase 3-positive cells at 8 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: Moreover, we also observed a significant decrease in caspase 3-positive cells at both time points (3 and 8 weeks post-viral treatment) in the lungs of Tert-treated mice compared to the empty-treated cohort (Figure 3A,B), indicative of decreased apoptosis.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Senescence epithelial cells were readily detected in mice diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and treated with the empty vector.
source: While senescence epithelial cells were readily detected in mice diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and treated with the empty vector, they were undetectable in the residual fibrotic areas present in few AAV9-Tert treated lungs at the end of the experiment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Senescent epithelial cells were undetectable in the residual fibrotic areas present in few AAV9-Tert treated lungs at the end of the experiment.
source: While senescence epithelial cells were readily detected in mice diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and treated with the empty vector, they were undetectable in the residual fibrotic areas present in few AAV9-Tert treated lungs at the end of the experiment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The amount of damaged ATII cells in AAV9-Tert treated lungs is reduced by 3-fold compared to control mice treated with the AAV9-Empty vector at 3 weeks post-viral treatment.
source: The results clearly show that the amount of damaged ATII cells in AAV9-Tert treated lungs is reduced by 3-fold compared to control mice treated with the AAV9-Empty vector at 3 weeks post-viral treatment (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: ATII cells have shorter telomeres than non-ATII cells in telomerase-deficient mice.
source: We found that ATII cells have shorter telomeres than non-ATII cells in telomerase-deficient mice in agreement with our previous findings indicating that these cells are important for the regeneration of lung damage induced by dysfunctional telomeres, as they have undergone more cell divisions (Povedano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data, supported by citation to Povedano et al., 2015.

claim: ATII cells from mice treated with AAV9-Tert showed the same telomere length as the surrounding non-ATII cells.
source: Interestingly, ATII cells from mice treated with AAV9-Tert showed the same telomere length than the surrounding non-ATII cells, suggesting that telomerase treatment is preserving telomeres in these cells in the context of lung fibrosis (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: The percentage of short telomeres of ATII cells compared to non-ATII in empty vector-treated mice (ATII/non-ATII ratio = 1.4) is significantly higher than in AAV9-Tert treated mice (ATII/non-ATII ratio = 0.98).
source: Indeed, the percentage of short telomeres of ATII cells compared to non-ATII in empty vector-treated mice (ATII/non-ATII ratio = 1.4) is significantly higher than in AAV9-Tert treated mice (ATII/non-ATII ratio = 0.98).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from telomere analysis.

claim: Tert treated mice showed a 2-fold increase in Ki67 positive cells in whole lung tissue compared to controls.
source: We found that Tert treated mice showed a 2-fold increase in Ki67 positive cells in whole lung tissue compared to controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated lungs showed a 2-fold increase in the total number of Sftpc positive cells compared to the empty vector controls.
source: When specifically looking at ATII cells, we observed a 2-fold increase in the total number of Sftpc positive cells and 2.5-fold increase in Ki67 positive ATII cells in AAV9-Tert treated lungs compared to the empty vector controls (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: AAV9-Tert treated lungs showed a 2.5-fold increase in Ki67 positive ATII cells compared to the empty vector controls.
source: When specifically looking at ATII cells, we observed a 2-fold increase in the total number of Sftpc positive cells and 2.5-fold increase in Ki67 positive ATII cells in AAV9-Tert treated lungs compared to the empty vector controls (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: 80% of the total AAV9-infected lung cells are ATII cells.
source: Although we cannot distinguish between the AAV9-Tert infected and non-infected ATII cells, the fact that 80% of the total AAV9-infected lung cells are ATII cells (Figure 1A), suggests that AAV9-Tert treatment is resulting in increased proliferation of these cells leading to a higher potential for lung regeneration and the remission of lung fibrosis.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Only 53 genes were significantly upregulated (FDR < 0.05) in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to mice treated with the empty vector.
source: We found that only 53 genes were significantly upregulated (False Discovery Rate, FDR < 0.05) in AAV9-Tert treated mice compared to mice treated with the empty vector (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from microarray analysis.

claim: Pathways upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis.
source: Those pathways found upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis, apoptosis, DNA repair, the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway, and extension of telomeres (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs included apoptosis pathways.
source: Those pathways found upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis, apoptosis, DNA repair, the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway, and extension of telomeres (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs included DNA repair pathways.
source: Those pathways found upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis, apoptosis, DNA repair, the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway, and extension of telomeres (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs included the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway.
source: Those pathways found upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis, apoptosis, DNA repair, the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway, and extension of telomeres (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs included extension of telomeres pathway.
source: Those pathways found upregulated in AAV9-Tert treated lungs presented a signature related with DNA replication and mitosis, apoptosis, DNA repair, the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway, and extension of telomeres (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs were related to fibroblast growth factor receptors.
source: In contrast, pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs were related to fibroblast growth factor receptors, Wnt and TGF-β pathways (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs included Wnt pathway.
source: In contrast, pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs were related to fibroblast growth factor receptors, Wnt and TGF-β pathways (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs included TGF-β pathway.
source: In contrast, pathways downregulated in AAV9-Tert compared to AAV9-Empty treated lungs were related to fibroblast growth factor receptors, Wnt and TGF-β pathways (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four of the pathways downregulated by Tert are related with fibroblast growth factor receptors: FGFR2C, FGFR4, FGFR and the FGFR1 ligand binding and activation cascades.
source: Of interest, four of the pathways downregulated by Tert are related with fibroblast growth factor receptors; that is, the FGFR2C, FGFR4, FGFR and the FGFR1 ligand binding and activation cascades (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FGF1-FGFRc over-expression has been shown to contribute to pathogenesis in IPF patients.
source: As FGF1-FGFRc over-expression has been shown to contribute to pathogenesis in IPF patients (MacKenzie et al., 2015), these findings suggest that Tert impairs fibroblast activation, thus facilitating fibrosis regression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacKenzie et al., 2015.

claim: Tert overexpression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) induces downregulation of TGF-β.
source: This is in agreement with our previous findings that Tert overexpression in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) induces downregulation of TGF-β (Geserick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geserick et al., 2006.

claim: TGF-β pathway has been linked to fibroblast activation and differentiation to myofibroblast.
source: TGF-β pathway has been linked to fibroblast activation and differentiation to myofibroblast (Pedroza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pedroza et al., 2016.

claim: Pirfenidone, a drug that blocks TGF-β, can significantly slow pulmonary fibrosis progression.
source: Indeed, pirfenidone, a drug that blocks TGF-β can significantly slow pulmonary fibrosis progression (Hunninghake, 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; King et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hunninghake, 2014; Karimi-Shah and Chowdhury, 2015; and King et al., 2014.

claim: High levels of the Wnt pathway genes Lrp5 and Lrp6 are linked to bad prognosis for IPF patients.
source: Instead, our results go in line with recent findings showing that high levels of the Wnt pathway genes Lrp5 and Lrp6 are linked to bad prognosis for IPF patients (Lam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lam et al., 2014.

claim: Mmp9 overexpression attenuates fibrosis in bleomycin-induced IPF.
source: Interestingly, we found Mmp9 upregulation in Tert treated lungs, in line with the fact that Mmp9 overexpression attenuates fibrosis in bleomycin-induced IPF (Cabrera et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cabrera et al., 2007.

claim: Most upregulated genes in AAV9-Tert treated lungs corresponded to genes specifically expressed by ATII cells.
source: Most upregulated genes (0 < Fc < 1) corresponded to genes specifically expressed by ATII cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), with a minority of the genes being normally expressed in leukocytes or embryonic fibroblasts.
evidence: This is based on comparison with The Gene Expression Barcode 3.0, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FACS-sorted ATII cells from AAV9-Tert treated mice showed Tert mRNA expression while it was undetectable in FACS-sorted ATII cells from empty vector-treated controls.
source: FACS-sorted ATII cells from AAV9-Tert treated mice showed Tert mRNA expression while it was undetectable in FACS-sorted ATII cells from empty vector-treated controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ATII cells from Tert treated mice showed decreased p53 mRNA expression compared with empty vector treated mice.
source: We also validated decreased p53 and p21 mRNA expression by RT-PCR in ATII cells from Tert treated mice compared with empty vector treated mice (Figure 5D,E), in agreement with lower senescence and DNA damage in Tert treated mice (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: ATII cells from Tert treated mice showed decreased p21 mRNA expression compared with empty vector treated mice.
source: We also validated decreased p53 and p21 mRNA expression by RT-PCR in ATII cells from Tert treated mice compared with empty vector treated mice (Figure 5D,E), in agreement with lower senescence and DNA damage in Tert treated mice (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: GSEA analysis of isolated ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of p53 signaling pathways.
source: Importantly, upon gene expression analysis of isolated ATII cells from Tert-treated mice, GSEA analysis showed downregulation of p53 signaling and apoptotic pathways (Figure 5F,G), consistent with lower DNA damage in lungs from Tert-treated mice compared to those from empty vector-treated mice (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: GSEA analysis of isolated ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of apoptotic pathways.
source: Importantly, upon gene expression analysis of isolated ATII cells from Tert-treated mice, GSEA analysis showed downregulation of p53 signaling and apoptotic pathways (Figure 5F,G), consistent with lower DNA damage in lungs from Tert-treated mice compared to those from empty vector-treated mice (see Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of TGF-β signaling pathway.
source: Also in line with lower fibrosis in the lungs from Tert- treated mice, ATII cells showed downregulation of several inflammation related pathways including the TGF-β, NF-KappaB, IL2 and TNF signaling pathways (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of NF-KappaB signaling pathway.
source: Also in line with lower fibrosis in the lungs from Tert- treated mice, ATII cells showed downregulation of several inflammation related pathways including the TGF-β, NF-KappaB, IL2 and TNF signaling pathways (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of IL2 signaling pathway.
source: Also in line with lower fibrosis in the lungs from Tert- treated mice, ATII cells showed downregulation of several inflammation related pathways including the TGF-β, NF-KappaB, IL2 and TNF signaling pathways (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: ATII cells from Tert-treated mice showed downregulation of TNF signaling pathway.
source: Also in line with lower fibrosis in the lungs from Tert- treated mice, ATII cells showed downregulation of several inflammation related pathways including the TGF-β, NF-KappaB, IL2 and TNF signaling pathways (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Wild-type mice inoculated with the standard high-dose bleomycin protocol did not show any significant telomere length changes 4 weeks after bleomycin challenge compared to vehicle inoculated mice.
source: In particular, we show here that male wild-type mice inoculated either with vehicle or with the standard high-dose bleomycin protocol did not show any significant telomere length changes 4 weeks after bleomycin challenge compared to vehicle inoculated mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that this mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis does not recapitulate one of the molecular features of the human disease (ie, the presence of short telomeres).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The high-dose bleomycin mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis does not recapitulate the presence of short telomeres seen in human disease.
source: In particular, we show here that male wild-type mice inoculated either with vehicle or with the standard high-dose bleomycin protocol did not show any significant telomere length changes 4 weeks after bleomycin challenge compared to vehicle inoculated mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that this mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis does not recapitulate one of the molecular features of the human disease (ie, the presence of short telomeres).
evidence: This is inferred from the telomere length data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of wild-type mice with high-dose bleomycin and AAV9-Tert did not show any significant decrease in the amount of fibronectin compared to the empty vector-treated lungs.
source: Further supporting this notion, treatment of these mice with AAV9-Tert did not show any significant decrease in the amount of fibronectin compared to the empty vector-treated lungs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AAV9-Tert transduced lungs cells showed Tert mRNA over-expression for at least 8 months post-infection of the vector.
source: In particular, we previously showed that AAV9-Tert transduced lungs cells showed Tert mRNA over-expression for at least 8 month post-infection of the vector, as well as resulted in re-activation of telomerase as determined by Telomerase Repeated Amplification Protocol (TRAP) in adult lungs (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012.

claim: AAV9-Tert transduction resulted in re-activation of telomerase as determined by TRAP in adult lungs.
source: In particular, we previously showed that AAV9-Tert transduced lungs cells showed Tert mRNA over-expression for at least 8 month post-infection of the vector, as well as resulted in re-activation of telomerase as determined by Telomerase Repeated Amplification Protocol (TRAP) in adult lungs (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012.

claim: ATII cells have been proposed to be involved in lung regeneration upon injuries.
source: ATII cells have been also proposed to be involved in lung regeneration upon injuries (Serrano-Mollar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serrano-Mollar et al., 2007.

claim: IPF is the result of defective regeneration upon repetitive epithelial cell injury.
source: These results are in line with the notion that short telomeres can impair the ability of stem cells to regenerate tissues (Blasco, 2007; Flores et al., 2008), and with recent findings suggesting that IPF is the result of defective regeneration upon repetitive epithelial cell injury (Hinz et al., 2007; Ryu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hinz et al., 2007 and Ryu et al., 2014.

claim: Treatment with GRN510, a small molecule activator of telomerase, suppresses the development of fibrosis and accumulation of senescent cells in the lung in a model of bleomycin-induced fibrosis.
source: In agreement with this, it was shown that treatment with GRN510, a small molecule activator of telomerase, suppresses the development of fibrosis and accumulation of senescent cells in the lung in a model of bleomycin-induced fibrosis (Le Saux et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Le Saux et al., 2013.

claim: Transcriptional active host loci and DNA repair factors impact on rAAV vector integration in the host genome.
source: As a note of caution regarding the use of AAV vectors, it has been shown that transcriptional active host loci and DNA repair factors impact on rAAV vector integration in the host genome as well as on vector maintenance as linear or circular episomes, affecting thereby the duration of expression and mutagenic potential of the vector (Inagaki et al., 2007; Nakai et al., 2003; Song et al., 2001; Song et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Inagaki et al., 2007; Nakai et al., 2003; Song et al., 2001; and Song et al., 2004.

claim: DNA repair factors impact on vector maintenance as linear or circular episomes, affecting the duration of expression and mutagenic potential of the vector.
source: As a note of caution regarding the use of AAV vectors, it has been shown that transcriptional active host loci and DNA repair factors impact on rAAV vector integration in the host genome as well as on vector maintenance as linear or circular episomes, affecting thereby the duration of expression and mutagenic potential of the vector (Inagaki et al., 2007; Nakai et al., 2003; Song et al., 2001; Song et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Inagaki et al., 2007; Nakai et al., 2003; Song et al., 2001; and Song et al., 2004.

claim: No increased cancer incidence was observed by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in AAV9-Tert treatment to delay organismal aging and increase longevity.
source: In addition, although we have not observed increased cancer incidence by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in different mouse models previously studied in the lab, such as AAV9-Tert treatment to delay organismal aging and increase longevity (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012), AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of heart infarct (Bär et al., 2014), and AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of aplastic anemia (Bar et al., 2016), further work is needed to address its potential tumorigenic effects in cancer prone scenarios, or in the context of severely damaged tissues, where senescence and apoptosis may be acting as tumor suppressive mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012.

claim: No increased cancer incidence was observed by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of heart infarct.
source: In addition, although we have not observed increased cancer incidence by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in different mouse models previously studied in the lab, such as AAV9-Tert treatment to delay organismal aging and increase longevity (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012), AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of heart infarct (Bär et al., 2014), and AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of aplastic anemia (Bar et al., 2016), further work is needed to address its potential tumorigenic effects in cancer prone scenarios, or in the context of severely damaged tissues, where senescence and apoptosis may be acting as tumor suppressive mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bär et al., 2014.

claim: No increased cancer incidence was observed by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of aplastic anemia.
source: In addition, although we have not observed increased cancer incidence by systemic administration of the AAV9-Tert vector in different mouse models previously studied in the lab, such as AAV9-Tert treatment to delay organismal aging and increase longevity (Bernardes de Jesus et al., 2012), AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of heart infarct (Bär et al., 2014), and AAV9-Tert treatment in mouse models of aplastic anemia (Bar et al., 2016), further work is needed to address its potential tumorigenic effects in cancer prone scenarios, or in the context of severely damaged tissues, where senescence and apoptosis may be acting as tumor suppressive mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bar et al., 2016.

claim: AAV9 serotype has high viral transduction of the lungs.
source: To test the efficacy of telomerase gene therapy in our mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis induced by DNA damage to the lungs (ie.,low-dose bleomycin) and the presence of short telomeres (Povedano et al., 2015), we selected AAV9 serotype owing to its high viral transduction of the lungs, and its low immunogenicity (Bell et al., 2011; Zincarelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2011 and Zincarelli et al., 2008.

claim: AAV9 serotype has low immunogenicity.
source: To test the efficacy of telomerase gene therapy in our mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis induced by DNA damage to the lungs (ie.,low-dose bleomycin) and the presence of short telomeres (Povedano et al., 2015), we selected AAV9 serotype owing to its high viral transduction of the lungs, and its low immunogenicity (Bell et al., 2011; Zincarelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2011 and Zincarelli et al., 2008.

claim: The reported abundance of ATII cells in whole lung cell population is 12–15%.
source: We first observed that 13.4% of total lung cells were ATII cells (Sftpc-positive cells) (Figure 1A), which is in line with the 12–15% reported abundance of ATII cells in whole lung cell population (Dobbs, 1990; Van der Velden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dobbs, 1990 and Van der Velden et al., 2013.

claim: Telomerase activation may represent an effective treatment for pulmonary fibrosis provoked or associated with short telomeres.
source: We provide a proof-of-principle that telomerase activation may represent an effective treatment for pulmonary fibrosis provoked or associated with short telomeres.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.
